Post Elections - What Now?

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The people of South Africa have spoken, heralding the brand new dawn with Cyril Ramaphosa at the helm of the ANC. Is it time for action or just more of the same?

Unique Selling Point:
The Brand New Dawn is upon us with Cyril Ramaphosa at the helm of the ruling party, the ANC. The ANC has lost 12% of the share of the vote since the 2004 elections, showing dwindling support and belief in the party by South African citizens. Many attribute the ANC’s win to the man himself Cyril Ramaphosa.
Disgruntled citizens together with a divided ANC... how can one man bring unity to a party that is factionalised and put into action promises that have been made to the electorate? Is Cyril Ramaphosa really the man of the hour, and can he last long enough in office to implement his vision? Carte Blanche speaks to insiders and analysts who consider whether the President can shine light on the fortunes of ordinary South Africans or if competing ANC factionalism will snuff out hope.

Summary:
South Africa has had its 6th free election, 25 years on from 1994. The African National Congress winning 57.5% of the vote, but showing dwindling support for the party, amidst a backdrop of a failing economy, corruption and record breaking unemployment rates. Experts tout Ramaphoria as a key factor to the ANC retaining its majority. But is Cyril Ramaphosa the man for the job, and how telling will be the internal politics within the ANC when it comes to choosing his cabinet. Will he be reigned in by internal forces or will he declare war and risk losing support within his own party? Can Cyril Ramaphosa change the perception of the ANC and put measures in place that will improve the lives of South Africans? Is he able to turn the economy around in time for South Africa to avoid another downgrade to junk status?
Political and economic analysts dissect the issues and warn about the challenges, but we get an inside track on Ramaphosa the man by Ronnie Kasrils who has seen him in action going back to the Bisho Massacre in 1992 and has seen him in action within the ANC.

In the announcement of his presidency in 2018, Ramaphosa announce his New Dawn, setting key objectives and goals for the country: tackling joblessness and corruption head-on, accelerating the pace of land redistribution and driving up investment in South Africa.

Ramaphosa’s central pledge of the 2019 election is to build an inclusive economy that will address the big five crises facing ordinary South Africans: corruption, the lack of basic service delivery, unemployment, inequality and poverty. We go directly to Luthuli House and ask how he plans on furthering those objectives in the “Brand New Dawn” and what would be his immediate challenges and tasks. Carte Blanche takes a critical look at South Africa’s deepening social and political divides and the man tasked to make the changes that South Africans have been waiting 25 years for.

Further information:
Background Info and interviews:

Aubrey: When we look at the 2019 election results we have to go back to 2004 and put it in context. The ANC has lost 12% since it’s 69,69% win in 2004. If they keep with the same trajectory they will lose power in the next 3 elections.

The elections don’t tell a good story with regard to race relations on an intra and an inter racial level, as seen in how many votes the FFP got.

Basically the black voters that had migrated to the DA left and the white voters who were only voting to oppose the ANC switched to the FFP.

There is no non racialism project in South Africa, race relations have never been worse.

Youth unemployment - economists are not asking the right questions. The premise has been you need growth to get jobs. If you look at it historically growth does not necessarily mean jobs, growth can be investment into industries that are automated, which won’t necessarily yield jobs. The question people should be asking the economists is, how do we create jobs? Once we have created jobs we can see growth.

With regards to the Ramaphosa presidency, it is a myth that he has a free hand, he needs the patronage of his supporters and his detractors within the party and that is a difficult balancing act that he has to do.

For example, he will find it difficult to get rid of Bathabile Dlamini as he needs the Women’s League and their support. If he bites the bullet and does not include her in the his new cabinet structure there could be a serious backlash within the ANC.

The State Capture commission is only scheduled to be finalised in 2020, and could even be postponed to 2021, so those who are baying for accountability when it comes to State Capture findings may have to wait for a while. And it is a trend globally with these kinds of enquiries that the small fish are sacrificed in order take the fall for the big fish who will ultimately continue without any consequence.

According to Aubrey, the Guptas, Bossassa merely interrupted the main actors in State Capture. The best way of looting in any country is to manipulate the content of policy.

One has to just take the global report of Price Waterhouse Cooper on the Global Economic Crime and Fraud Survey, 2018 where South Africa has reported the highest percentage of economic crime in the world, followed by Kenya and France.

Education is going to continue being a problem, and South Africa is rated amongst the worst countries in the world, coming 3rd last in maths and science. Most high school teachers are not qualified to teach maths and science. Unfortunately SATU is a big problem and is not progressive in terms of changing the environment, too many self interests. The ANC are not willing to cross SATU, as they depend on their members for votes and support. So little can be done to change the educational front. And now tertiary education doesn’t even guarantee jobs.

Economically within the bigger context still retains a Victorian structure. So South Africa still, in essence, belongs to the people who conquered it. This needs to change so that South Africans can have economic enfranchisement.

As far as Aubrey is concerned, Ramaphosa is not the answer. He does not have enough strength within the ANC.

Thabi Leoka - Economist, is on the shortlist for the President’s Dream Team, who are going to advise on all aspects of the economy going forward. This panel was set up during Thabo Mbeki’s presidency and then disbanded in the Zuma era. Ramaphosa is bringing it back.

Thabi says, in order to create growth we need job creation, and there has to be a creative approach to job creation, as she also believes that growth does not necessarily yield jobs.

There are three key industries that have been neglected in South Africa that do not require a high level of education. And that is the mining sector, agriculture and manufacturing sector that have been severely neglected. They can provide more jobs, especially if South Africa makes use of the Africa Free Trade Agreement by, for example, manufacturing in rail and transport, as well as road infrastructure.

These industries can be supported and boosted with financial support and access to markets.

Thabi will also speak on the Moody’s warning, if South Africa can’t slow down the rising debt and boost the economic growth the country could be downgraded to sub investment level, which is basically junk status. Moody’s is currently the only major rating agency that has the country’s sovereign debt above junk, and November is the next review.

Signs of not being able to cope with shocks to the economy, central to this is Eskom, central to debt and pivotal for economic growth.

Ronnie Kasrils - prominent member of the ANC (member of the NEC, 1987 - 2007): Ronnie Kasrils will talk in personal terms about the man Cyril Ramaphosa and his feelings about Ramaphosa's character and whether or not he is the right man for South Africa's main job. As far back as the Bisho Massacre of 1992, Ronnie Kasrils has walked arm in arm with Cyril Ramaphosa in the ANC. A communist at heart, he may be on a competing economic tack with the President, but when it comes to the corruption and state capture of the Zuma years, the two men, at least publicly, stand shoulder to shoulder in defence of good governance. Former Intelligence Minister Kasrils has recently heaped praise on the report of Ramaphosa's review panel on the State Security Agency (SSA).

Luthuli House: We ask the ANC themselves about the President and what his immediate challenges will be once taking up office. What his plans are and what we should be looking forward to as ordinary South Africans. We put to Luthuli House, how do they see Cyril Ramaphosa taking South Africans into the Brand New Dawn.

Expert:
Mr. Aubrey Matshiqi Political analyst
Ms. Thabi Leoka
Mr. Ronnie Kasrils
Ms. Khusela Sangoni
Ms. Trudi Makhaya

Press Release:


Ramaphosa Post-Election
The post-election dawn has broken with a widely respected Cyril Ramaphosa entrenched by popular vote at the helm of the country. As he constructs his new cabinet from a divided ANC and hammers out its first priorities, how is the president approaching a failing economy, State-sponsored corruption and record-breaking unemployment rates? Carte Blanche examines what the president’s powers and prerogatives are as he grapples with turning the country’s fortunes around.
Producer: Sophia Phirippides
Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


Inauguration footage… sound up then cover next bit of link...

VO: Replace link:
The brand new dawn is upon us with the inauguration of President Matamela Cyril Ramaphosa, a vote of confidence by the people, in South Africa’s 6th democratic election.


Beat: Sound up inauguration …

LINK: Since the 2004 elections, support for the party has been dwindling, losing 12% of the national vote but many have attributed the ANC's 2019 general elections win to the man himself, president Cyril Ramaphosa.

More inauguration footage out…

Ronnie: People were feeling “Wow we have to have Ramaphosa back, it’s the only hope for SA. His victory has lightened the situation up for all of us, it was looking so dark and bleak.

VO: Struggle stalwart Ronnie Kasrils, has worked closely with Cyril Ramaphosa, having seen him in action going back to the Bisho Massacre in 1992, and witnessed him rise within the ranks of the ANC.

Ronnie: He's a superb chess player, Cyril is thinking things out, he's measuring the individual, I’m talking politically there’s different factors, so he's got to measure the person, what the agenda is and the situation, the context and he does that in a very sophisticated manner. He's not the two faced stab you in the back while smiling, that’s not Ramaphosa.

Masa: You wrote a book about former president Jacob Zuma titled A Simple Man. If you had to write a book about Ramaphosa having worked so closely with him, what would you title it?

Ronnie: Maybe The Congenial Man.

Ronnie: That’s the first word that came out. But he's so engaging, you relax with Cyril Ramaphosa, he's warm, he’s personable and he's very genuine.

LINK: South Africans may be caught in the aftermath of Ramaphoria, but skeptics aren't convinced that the man of the hour has what it takes to withstand the backlash of his internal party politics.

VO: Least of all, Political Analyst Prince Mashele who warns that President Cyril Ramaphosa should ready himself for a tough fight.

Prince: The factions within the ANC will do their best, that Cyril Ramaphosa does not succeed in rebuilding state institutions, because they know if we have strong institutions they’re going to jail, they will fight very hard to make sure that government is ungovernable, so we must expect turbulence.

Ronnie: He's got to clear out the rot and with it unify the party behind his leadership

Prince: My sense is that Ramaphosa will try and manage the mess in the ANC by not rocking the boat because he knows if he rocks the boat the thugs are going to come for him.

Ronnie: I think he's a person of integrity and courage although people say where's the courage, lets see because the chips are down now and he’s got to really show that he is going to be decisive and he's got to do it for his own sake, but really for the country’s

VO: President Ramaphosa has his work cut out for him, in driving through the reforms that fulfil his central pledge of the 2019 election - to build an inclusive economy that will address corruption, the lack of basic service delivery, unemployment, inequality and poverty, in a country hungry for economic freedom after 25 years of democracy.

And Economist Xhanti Payi stresses the need to evolve with global shifts.

Xhanti: If we think about the industrial revolution we're in, whether it’s fourth or fifth industrial revolution, reform is about how we make sure that we are fit to enter that area so how we rethink everything. How do we make sure our environment is in such a space that it allows us to attract more investment from outside, and the kind of promises we can make them.

VO: Ramaphosa’s track record has proven him to be a friend of big business having already yielded results in his investment drive, with inflows more than doubling in 2018 according to the Reserve Bank.

Prince: It doesn’t matter that business is fond of Ramaphosa. If you are in the township and you are black, you have no skills, you have not been to school. Ramaphosa can have a nice dinner with his business friends, that is not going to create a factory in your neighborhood. Period. If you look at SA economically you will realize we are not competitive internationally. The current level of investment and economic activity in SA is not enough to reduce unemployment which is why statistics are worsening by the day.

LINK: Poverty and inequality have become endemic to our country's landscape. According to Stats SA 6.2 million South Africans are unemployed. This has the potential to stunt any future economic growth

Prince: If you continue to have schools that are dysfunctional they will produce unemployable, uneducated and unskilled young SA. So the biggest challenge facing Ramaphosa is the question of the economy and I don’t see him turning it around.

Xhanti: There was a time we thought, you know, grow the economy and it will trickle down to everyone and it will feed the poor. I think that has been largely debunked. Actually the reason we are not growing is because people are not working. We must first put people to work so we can demonstrate that our economy has potential.

VO: Economists are of the opinion that declining sectors, such as manufacturing, can become potential areas for growth with the right support from the Ramaphosa government.

Xhanti: In his investment summit where there were actually presentations of the kinds of areas where he thinks we should be focusing. Of course mining has been one of them, financial services is something that can’t be left behind, we know agriculture will be big because it’s also about the question of land and how we actually make sure that there we reform that legislation.

Masa: What is the single greatest threat to our economy?

Xhanti: A downgrade is one of the most dangerous things we face

VO: Moody’s, the only major ratings agency to have South Africa above junk status, has its next rating review in November. And Eskom’s debt of over 400 billion rand continues to threaten to destabilize the economy.

Xhanti: This whole idea that eskom is our biggest problem, actually energy is our biggest problem and if we think about it from that perspective then we are starting to think about it in different ways.

LINK: There's been a lot of talk about rooting out corruption and cleaning up state owned entities, we've seen commissions in action with shocking revelations, but how much is within the president's power going forward?

Prince: Cyril Ramaphosa presides over state institutions so if he gives an instruction to the NPA, to the police and say arrest without fear or favour, prosecute. Those institutions can bite. . But in the economy he doesn’t have direct control.

VO: So as he starts his tenure, ultimately President Ramaphosa’s power lies in his choice of cabinet, signalling his agenda for the next five years.

Prince: He must remove rotten apples from his cabinet appoint credible people in credible positions, such as finance. Public enterprises, our state owned enterprises are broken they need to be fixed.

VO: In his inauguration address, President Matamela Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged the many challenges facing South Africa, but vowed that there would be a better tomorrow for all its people.

Ronnie: I don’t think there's anybody better at present capable of turning the tide. If he can get this population behind him then he's a giant, then he can move mountains.

Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 07 June 2019 Press Release: Ramaphosa Post-Election The post-election dawn has broken with a widely respected Cyril Ramaphosa entrenched by popular vote at the helm of the country. As he constructs his new cabinet from a divided ANC and hammers out its first priorities, how is the president approaching a failing economy, State-sponsored corruption and record-breaking unemployment rates? Carte Blanche examines what the president’s powers and prerogatives are as he grapples with turning the country’s fortunes around. Producer: Sophia Phirippides Presenter: Masa Kekana Script: Inauguration footage… sound up then cover next bit of link... VO: Replace link: The brand new dawn is upon us with the inauguration of President Matamela Cyril Ramaphosa, a vote of confidence by the people, in South Africa’s 6th democratic election. Beat: Sound up inauguration … LINK: Since the 2004 elections, support for the party has been dwindling, losing 12% of the national vote but many have attributed the ANC's 2019 general elections win to the man himself, president Cyril Ramaphosa. More inauguration footage out… Ronnie: People were feeling “Wow we have to have Ramaphosa back, it’s the only hope for SA. His victory has lightened the situation up for all of us, it was looking so dark and bleak. VO: Struggle stalwart Ronnie Kasrils, has worked closely with Cyril Ramaphosa, having seen him in action going back to the Bisho Massacre in 1992, and witnessed him rise within the ranks of the ANC. Ronnie: He's a superb chess player, Cyril is thinking things out, he's measuring the individual, I’m talking politically there’s different factors, so he's got to measure the person, what the agenda is and the situation, the context and he does that in a very sophisticated manner. He's not the two faced stab you in the back while smiling, that’s not Ramaphosa. Masa: You wrote a book about former president Jacob Zuma titled A Simple Man. If you had to write a book about Ramaphosa having worked so closely with him, what would you title it? Ronnie: Maybe The Congenial Man. Ronnie: That’s the first word that came out. But he's so engaging, you relax with Cyril Ramaphosa, he's warm, he’s personable and he's very genuine. LINK: South Africans may be caught in the aftermath of Ramaphoria, but skeptics aren't convinced that the man of the hour has what it takes to withstand the backlash of his internal party politics. VO: Least of all, Political Analyst Prince Mashele who warns that President Cyril Ramaphosa should ready himself for a tough fight. Prince: The factions within the ANC will do their best, that Cyril Ramaphosa does not succeed in rebuilding state institutions, because they know if we have strong institutions they’re going to jail, they will fight very hard to make sure that government is ungovernable, so we must expect turbulence. Ronnie: He's got to clear out the rot and with it unify the party behind his leadership Prince: My sense is that Ramaphosa will try and manage the mess in the ANC by not rocking the boat because he knows if he rocks the boat the thugs are going to come for him. Ronnie: I think he's a person of integrity and courage although people say where's the courage, lets see because the chips are down now and he’s got to really show that he is going to be decisive and he's got to do it for his own sake, but really for the country’s VO: President Ramaphosa has his work cut out for him, in driving through the reforms that fulfil his central pledge of the 2019 election - to build an inclusive economy that will address corruption, the lack of basic service delivery, unemployment, inequality and poverty, in a country hungry for economic freedom after 25 years of democracy. And Economist Xhanti Payi stresses the need to evolve with global shifts. Xhanti: If we think about the industrial revolution we're in, whether it’s fourth or fifth industrial revolution, reform is about how we make sure that we are fit to enter that area so how we rethink everything. How do we make sure our environment is in such a space that it allows us to attract more investment from outside, and the kind of promises we can make them. VO: Ramaphosa’s track record has proven him to be a friend of big business having already yielded results in his investment drive, with inflows more than doubling in 2018 according to the Reserve Bank. Prince: It doesn’t matter that business is fond of Ramaphosa. If you are in the township and you are black, you have no skills, you have not been to school. Ramaphosa can have a nice dinner with his business friends, that is not going to create a factory in your neighborhood. Period. If you look at SA economically you will realize we are not competitive internationally. The current level of investment and economic activity in SA is not enough to reduce unemployment which is why statistics are worsening by the day. LINK: Poverty and inequality have become endemic to our country's landscape. According to Stats SA 6.2 million South Africans are unemployed. This has the potential to stunt any future economic growth Prince: If you continue to have schools that are dysfunctional they will produce unemployable, uneducated and unskilled young SA. So the biggest challenge facing Ramaphosa is the question of the economy and I don’t see him turning it around. Xhanti: There was a time we thought, you know, grow the economy and it will trickle down to everyone and it will feed the poor. I think that has been largely debunked. Actually the reason we are not growing is because people are not working. We must first put people to work so we can demonstrate that our economy has potential. VO: Economists are of the opinion that declining sectors, such as manufacturing, can become potential areas for growth with the right support from the Ramaphosa government. Xhanti: In his investment summit where there were actually presentations of the kinds of areas where he thinks we should be focusing. Of course mining has been one of them, financial services is something that can’t be left behind, we know agriculture will be big because it’s also about the question of land and how we actually make sure that there we reform that legislation. Masa: What is the single greatest threat to our economy? Xhanti: A downgrade is one of the most dangerous things we face VO: Moody’s, the only major ratings agency to have South Africa above junk status, has its next rating review in November. And Eskom’s debt of over 400 billion rand continues to threaten to destabilize the economy. Xhanti: This whole idea that eskom is our biggest problem, actually energy is our biggest problem and if we think about it from that perspective then we are starting to think about it in different ways. LINK: There's been a lot of talk about rooting out corruption and cleaning up state owned entities, we've seen commissions in action with shocking revelations, but how much is within the president's power going forward? Prince: Cyril Ramaphosa presides over state institutions so if he gives an instruction to the NPA, to the police and say arrest without fear or favour, prosecute. Those institutions can bite. . But in the economy he doesn’t have direct control. VO: So as he starts his tenure, ultimately President Ramaphosa’s power lies in his choice of cabinet, signalling his agenda for the next five years. Prince: He must remove rotten apples from his cabinet appoint credible people in credible positions, such as finance. Public enterprises, our state owned enterprises are broken they need to be fixed. VO: In his inauguration address, President Matamela Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged the many challenges facing South Africa, but vowed that there would be a better tomorrow for all its people. Ronnie: I don’t think there's anybody better at present capable of turning the tide. If he can get this population behind him then he's a giant, then he can move mountains.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The people of South Africa have spoken, heralding the brand new dawn with Cyril Ramaphosa at the helm of the ANC. Is it time for action or just more of the same?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Brand New Dawn is upon us with Cyril Ramaphosa at the helm of the ruling party, the ANC. The ANC has lost 12% of the share of the vote since the 2004 elections, showing dwindling support and belief in the party by South African citizens. Many attribute the ANC’s win to the man himself Cyril Ramaphosa. Disgruntled citizens together with a divided ANC... how can one man bring unity to a party that is factionalised and put into action promises that have been made to the electorate? Is Cyril Ramaphosa really the man of the hour, and can he last long enough in office to implement his vision? Carte Blanche speaks to insiders and analysts who consider whether the President can shine light on the fortunes of ordinary South Africans or if competing ANC factionalism will snuff out hope.
metadata.Summary: South Africa has had its 6th free election, 25 years on from 1994. The African National Congress winning 57.5% of the vote, but showing dwindling support for the party, amidst a backdrop of a failing economy, corruption and record breaking unemployment rates. Experts tout Ramaphoria as a key factor to the ANC retaining its majority. But is Cyril Ramaphosa the man for the job, and how telling will be the internal politics within the ANC when it comes to choosing his cabinet. Will he be reigned in by internal forces or will he declare war and risk losing support within his own party? Can Cyril Ramaphosa change the perception of the ANC and put measures in place that will improve the lives of South Africans? Is he able to turn the economy around in time for South Africa to avoid another downgrade to junk status? Political and economic analysts dissect the issues and warn about the challenges, but we get an inside track on Ramaphosa the man by Ronnie Kasrils who has seen him in action going back to the Bisho Massacre in 1992 and has seen him in action within the ANC. In the announcement of his presidency in 2018, Ramaphosa announce his New Dawn, setting key objectives and goals for the country: tackling joblessness and corruption head-on, accelerating the pace of land redistribution and driving up investment in South Africa. Ramaphosa’s central pledge of the 2019 election is to build an inclusive economy that will address the big five crises facing ordinary South Africans: corruption, the lack of basic service delivery, unemployment, inequality and poverty. We go directly to Luthuli House and ask how he plans on furthering those objectives in the “Brand New Dawn” and what would be his immediate challenges and tasks. Carte Blanche takes a critical look at South Africa’s deepening social and political divides and the man tasked to make the changes that South Africans have been waiting 25 years for.
metadata.Further information: Background Info and interviews: Aubrey: When we look at the 2019 election results we have to go back to 2004 and put it in context. The ANC has lost 12% since it’s 69,69% win in 2004. If they keep with the same trajectory they will lose power in the next 3 elections. The elections don’t tell a good story with regard to race relations on an intra and an inter racial level, as seen in how many votes the FFP got. Basically the black voters that had migrated to the DA left and the white voters who were only voting to oppose the ANC switched to the FFP. There is no non racialism project in South Africa, race relations have never been worse. Youth unemployment - economists are not asking the right questions. The premise has been you need growth to get jobs. If you look at it historically growth does not necessarily mean jobs, growth can be investment into industries that are automated, which won’t necessarily yield jobs. The question people should be asking the economists is, how do we create jobs? Once we have created jobs we can see growth. With regards to the Ramaphosa presidency, it is a myth that he has a free hand, he needs the patronage of his supporters and his detractors within the party and that is a difficult balancing act that he has to do. For example, he will find it difficult to get rid of Bathabile Dlamini as he needs the Women’s League and their support. If he bites the bullet and does not include her in the his new cabinet structure there could be a serious backlash within the ANC. The State Capture commission is only scheduled to be finalised in 2020, and could even be postponed to 2021, so those who are baying for accountability when it comes to State Capture findings may have to wait for a while. And it is a trend globally with these kinds of enquiries that the small fish are sacrificed in order take the fall for the big fish who will ultimately continue without any consequence. According to Aubrey, the Guptas, Bossassa merely interrupted the main actors in State Capture. The best way of looting in any country is to manipulate the content of policy. One has to just take the global report of Price Waterhouse Cooper on the Global Economic Crime and Fraud Survey, 2018 where South Africa has reported the highest percentage of economic crime in the world, followed by Kenya and France. Education is going to continue being a problem, and South Africa is rated amongst the worst countries in the world, coming 3rd last in maths and science. Most high school teachers are not qualified to teach maths and science. Unfortunately SATU is a big problem and is not progressive in terms of changing the environment, too many self interests. The ANC are not willing to cross SATU, as they depend on their members for votes and support. So little can be done to change the educational front. And now tertiary education doesn’t even guarantee jobs. Economically within the bigger context still retains a Victorian structure. So South Africa still, in essence, belongs to the people who conquered it. This needs to change so that South Africans can have economic enfranchisement. As far as Aubrey is concerned, Ramaphosa is not the answer. He does not have enough strength within the ANC. Thabi Leoka - Economist, is on the shortlist for the President’s Dream Team, who are going to advise on all aspects of the economy going forward. This panel was set up during Thabo Mbeki’s presidency and then disbanded in the Zuma era. Ramaphosa is bringing it back. Thabi says, in order to create growth we need job creation, and there has to be a creative approach to job creation, as she also believes that growth does not necessarily yield jobs. There are three key industries that have been neglected in South Africa that do not require a high level of education. And that is the mining sector, agriculture and manufacturing sector that have been severely neglected. They can provide more jobs, especially if South Africa makes use of the Africa Free Trade Agreement by, for example, manufacturing in rail and transport, as well as road infrastructure. These industries can be supported and boosted with financial support and access to markets. Thabi will also speak on the Moody’s warning, if South Africa can’t slow down the rising debt and boost the economic growth the country could be downgraded to sub investment level, which is basically junk status. Moody’s is currently the only major rating agency that has the country’s sovereign debt above junk, and November is the next review. Signs of not being able to cope with shocks to the economy, central to this is Eskom, central to debt and pivotal for economic growth. Ronnie Kasrils - prominent member of the ANC (member of the NEC, 1987 - 2007): Ronnie Kasrils will talk in personal terms about the man Cyril Ramaphosa and his feelings about Ramaphosa's character and whether or not he is the right man for South Africa's main job. As far back as the Bisho Massacre of 1992, Ronnie Kasrils has walked arm in arm with Cyril Ramaphosa in the ANC. A communist at heart, he may be on a competing economic tack with the President, but when it comes to the corruption and state capture of the Zuma years, the two men, at least publicly, stand shoulder to shoulder in defence of good governance. Former Intelligence Minister Kasrils has recently heaped praise on the report of Ramaphosa's review panel on the State Security Agency (SSA). Luthuli House: We ask the ANC themselves about the President and what his immediate challenges will be once taking up office. What his plans are and what we should be looking forward to as ordinary South Africans. We put to Luthuli House, how do they see Cyril Ramaphosa taking South Africans into the Brand New Dawn.
